entries.title: Estimating the Economic Value of Supported Online Parent-Led Cognitive Behavioral Therapy to Prevent Child Anxiety Problems: Economic Evaluation of the MYCATS Cluster Randomized Controlled Trial
entries.abstract: Abstract Background Childhood anxiety disorders are common and lead to substantial negative long-term outcomes in various life domains. Although digital interventions for preventing childhood anxiety problems have been increasingly used in the recent decade, there is limited evidence documenting their cost-effectiveness (CE). Objective This study aimed to evaluate the CE of a parent-led online cognitive behavioral therapy with therapist support (OSI+TS) alongside usual school practice (USP), compared to USP alone for children aged 4‐7 years at risk of anxiety disorders identified through universal school screening. Methods The economic evaluation was conducted alongside the MYCATS trial (N=865), a parallel group, superiority cluster randomized trial across 95 primary or infant schools in England. Schools were randomized (1:1) to OSI+TS or USP, stratified by school-level deprivation. The primary analyses, at 12 months after randomization, considered child quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) as the health economic outcome, using both the UK adult and the Australia adolescent value sets, and costs were from the National Health Service and Personal Social Services perspective. Incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) were compared to the UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommended threshold of £20,000-£30,000 (£1=US $1.35 as of September 10, 2026) per QALY gained, as per predefined Health Economics Analysis Plan. Sensitivity analyses included a societal perspective and the application of the new NICE cost-effectiveness threshold. Results Children receiving OSI+TS gained 0.021 (95% CI 0.010-0.033; P <.001) and 0.043 (95% CI 0.021-0.064; P <.001) QALYs, respectively, for United Kingdom and Australia value sets, with an additional cost of £244.16 compared to school usual practice only, resulting in ICERs of £11,462.47 and £5,700.98, respectively. At the £20,000 threshold, OSI+TS had an 88.2% or 99.3% chance of being cost-effective. Conclusions OSI+TS is cost-effective compared to usual school provision, supporting its future implementation for children at risk of anxiety problems.

entries.title: Prevalence and Correlates of Internet Addiction and its Association with Anxiety among School-going Adolescents in Lucknow, India: A Cross-sectional Study
entries.abstract: Abstract Background: Internet addiction, defined as excessive and compulsive use of Internet-enabled devices, has emerged as an important public health concern due to its association with anxiety, emotional distress, and impaired daily functioning. In India, rapid digitalization and widespread access to smartphones and online platforms have significantly increased Internet use among adolescents, raising concerns about problematic usage patterns and their impact on mental health. Methods: A school-based cross-sectional study was conducted from June to December 2024 among 400 adolescents aged 12–18 years in Lucknow District, Uttar Pradesh, India. Participants were selected through a multistage stratified random sampling method from government and private schools. Data were collected through a questionnaire with Young’s Internet Addiction Test (IAT) and the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) scale. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 22.0, employing Chi-square tests and multivariable logistic regression. Results: Overall, 289 participants (72.25%) exhibited some degree of Internet addiction (IAT ≥31), while severe addiction in 4 participants (1%). Internet addiction showed significant associations with age, gender, school type, daily screen time, and anxiety severity (all P < 0.05). Multivariable analysis revealed higher odds of Internet addiction among adolescents aged 15–16 years, in private schools, longer screen time, and levels of anxiety. Female gender, higher parental education, private school attendance, and screen time exceeding 4 hours per day were identified as important risk factors. Conclusion: Internet addiction is highly prevalent among adolescents. Comprehensive school-based interventions, including mental health screening and awareness programs, are needed to promote healthy Internet use and psychological wellbeing.

entries.title: Social media exposure and anxiety and depression in young people: A systematic review and meta‐analysis of longitudinal and experimental studies
entries.abstract: OBJECTIVES: The aim of the current review was to comprehensively synthesize the evidence for the relationship between social media use and anxiety and depression symptoms in young people using data from robust methodological designs, namely, longitudinal and experimental studies. METHODS: PsycINFO, Web of Science, MEDLINE, Embase and Scopus databases were searched for peer-reviewed, English-language, longitudinal and experimental studies. Included studies measured SMU in terms of time or frequency of use, mainly via self-report, used standardized measures of depression and anxiety, and recruited samples ranging from 10 to 24 years of age. RESULTS: Screening retrieved 37 eligible studies that included 36 longitudinal observational studies and one experiment. Twelve studies examined depression outcomes (pooled r = .08, 95% CIs [0.04, 0.11]), and five studies examined anxiety (pooled r = 0.093, 95% CIs [0.059, 0.126]), showing very small linear effects. There were no moderating effects for year of publication, duration of follow-up or mean age of sample for the depression effects. CONCLUSIONS: Given the very weak relationships between SMU and the severity of anxiety and depression symptoms, SMU is unlikely to account for the contemporary youth mental health crisis. Further longitudinal research designed to examine potential non-monotonic relationships between SMU and adverse mental health outcomes is required, along with attention to other potential causes of increased prevalence of mental health problems in young people.
